papers.title: PAIR: Preference-Aligned Intent Retrieval for Premium People Recommendation at LinkedIn
papers.authors: Zhongkai Shangguan, Yanbin Kang, Yihan Cao, Ruijie Jiang, Qiannan Yin, Chang Yue, Zijian Zhou, Girish Kathalagiri, Changshuai Wei, Zhengming Xing
papers.abstract: General-purpose embeddings trained on profile similarity often misrank candidates in professional networks, where relevance is inherently complementary rather than symmetric. For example, job seekers usually engage with recruiters rather than peers with similar credentials. Current user recommendation systems are often built on profile similarity or social signals such as shared connections, which are effective in friend-oriented social networks where users tend to connect with similar people or within existing social circles. However, this does not hold in professional platforms like LinkedIn, where interactions are often goal-driven and cross-role interactions, requiring matching based on complementary intents rather than similarity or social proximity. In this paper, we propose Preference-Aligned Intent Retrieval, a retrieval framework that is designed to model user intent preference instead of profile similarity. Our approach is inspired by the preference-learning perspective of Direct Preference Optimization, but instantiates preference learning as an exposure-conditioned multi-negative contrastive objective over embeddings. This formulation simplifies training and scales efficiently to large candidate sets without requiring an explicit reference model. Furthermore, we incorporate user interaction history by aggregating click histories with positional encoding to capture temporal order, which enables constant-cost updates of user representations over a fixed history window, allowing new interactions to be incorporated without re-encoding history. As a result, personalization can be updated efficiently using lightweight CPU operations without repeated LLM inference during serving. We evaluate PAIR on LinkedIn's Premium retrieval task. A 0.6B parameter model achieves a MAR@100 of 0.45.
papers.summary: LinkedIn finds that for Premium people-browsemap retrieval, the production member embedding Holistic-171 only reaches MAR@100 0.288, and an off-the-shelf 0.6B LLM embedding scores 0.192—neither was trained under the exposure condition of who the viewer already saw. PAIR treats exposure as the conditioning for preference learning; a same-scale 0.6B model lifts MAR@100 to 0.450 (56% relative over Holistic, 2.3× over the base encoder). Online A/B on Premium Browsemaps: CTR +7.5%, Premium retention +2.1%, no measurable latency regression. ==Who you already saw is preference signal, not noise: condition the objective on exposure and a small model can beat a broad member vector==.

deep_reading.title: PAIR: Preference-Aligned Intent Retrieval for Premium People Recommendation at LinkedIn
deep_reading.content:
When a software engineer starts job hunting on LinkedIn, the clicks shift from fellow engineers to recruiters, hiring managers and HR. In professional networking, relevance is often **complementary rather than symmetric**, so general-purpose embeddings trained on profile similarity misrank candidates. In LinkedIn's offline evaluation, the production member embedding Holistic-171 reaches only 0.288 MAR@100 on Premium user retrieval, and an off-the-shelf 0.6B general LLM embedding does worse at 0.192. A LinkedIn team proposes PAIR (Preference-Aligned Intent Retrieval): ==build preference supervision from production exposure logs, who was clicked and who was not==, and add a click-history tower that can be updated cheaply. The 0.6B model reaches 0.450 MAR@100, a 56% relative gain over Holistic-171 and 2.3× the off-the-shelf base. In an online A/B test on LinkedIn Premium Browsemaps, click-through rate rises 7.5% and Premium retention 2.1%, with no measurable latency regression.

![PAIR's triple-tower architecture: the profile and document towers share parameters to encode the query user's and candidates' profiles; the history tower aggregates embeddings of recently clicked profiles with positional attention to represent short-term intent; the final query representation fuses static profile and dynamic intent by normalized addition, so history updates never re-encode the profile with the LLM.](figs/2610.30941/hf1.png)

## 1. The problem: professional recommendation is not about finding similar people

Premium Browsemaps is LinkedIn's people-recommendation module for Premium subscribers, shown on member profile pages. The profile visits it generates feed notifications such as "Who viewed your profile", which shape users' sense of Premium's value and their renewals. The system has two stages: attribute filters (location, industry, seniority, language) narrow the Premium member pool, embedding-based retrieval (EBR) pulls about 100 candidates, and a ranking model picks the 4 shown to the user.

Retrieval defines every candidate the ranker can see; intent-matching candidates missed at retrieval cannot be recovered by ranking. Yet general embeddings cluster people with similar backgrounds: job seekers actually want recruiters or hiring managers, business developers want prospective clients or partners, and recruiters want candidates with complementary skills. The authors frame the problem as preference ranking: for a query user $q$, a clicked candidate $d^+$ should score above an unclicked $d^-$.

Deploying at LinkedIn scale adds two engineering constraints. First, **intent is dynamic**: someone actively job-hunting this week may shift to casual networking next month, and re-encoding hundreds of millions of profiles with an LLM whenever history changes is infeasible in production. Second, recommendation surfaces have different latency, memory and storage budgets, so a single model must provide embeddings at several dimensions.

## 2. Method I: exposure-conditioned preference learning

Training data comes from historical Premium Browsemaps production logs. In each recommendation impression, the clicked candidate is the positive; each positive gets 3 negatives, preferring candidates **exposed in the same impression but not clicked** (hard negatives) and, when fewer than 3 exist, filling the rest with random active Premium members outside the exposed set (easy negatives).

The score is temperature-scaled cosine similarity $s(q,d)=\cos(\mathbf e_q^{\rm final},\mathbf e_d)/\tau$, and the objective is a multi-negative softmax loss:

$$\mathcal L_{\rm PAIR}=-\log\frac{\exp(s(q,d^+))}{\exp(s(q,d^+))+\sum_{i=1}^{K}\exp(s(q,d_i^-))}$$

The authors state plainly that this has the same computational form as multi-negative contrastive learning (InfoNCE). The idea is inspired by DPO's preference-learning perspective, but it is not a direct embedding-space instance of DPO: there is no reference policy and no token-level probability ratio. The difference lies in what the supervision means: exposed-but-unclicked candidates are options the live retriever actually considers, not ANN-mined neighbors. PAIR therefore learns "whom users prefer within the live exposure distribution", and needs no extra reference-model forward pass. The authors acknowledge the cost: preferences are only observed inside exposed sets, so PAIR inherits selection bias from the historical retrieval policy, which future exploration-aware sampling could mitigate.

The authors note that initial fine-tuning with standard contrastive learning beat the off-the-shelf model, but the embedding space stayed similarity-oriented: a job-seeking engineer was still matched to other engineers. That is what motivated exposure-based negatives.

## 3. Method II: a cheaply updatable triple-tower intent architecture

To separate stable identity (who the user is) from short-term intent (what they need now), PAIR uses three towers. The query profile tower and document tower share encoder parameters (base Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B), and the history tower aggregates precomputed profile embeddings. Profiles are serialized as structured text: headline, summary, positions, education, skills, certifications, patents, honors, publications and languages.

**History aggregation with positional attention (P-ATT).** Take the $K=10$ most recently clicked profiles, each with an embedding $\mathbf e_{h_i}$ precomputed by the same encoder. Attention weights are $\alpha_i\propto\exp(\mathbf w^\top(\mathbf e_{h_i}+{\rm PE}(i)))$, where ${\rm PE}(i)$ is a learned positional encoding and the latest click is $i=1$. The history vector is $\mathbf e_{\mathcal H}=\sum_i\alpha_i\mathbf e_{h_i}$. The attention is **deliberately query-agnostic**: it learns global recency and item-importance weights, so the history vector can be refreshed independently of the query profile tower. Query-conditioned attention would be more expressive but adds joint query-history computation and complicates serving.

**Normalized additive fusion.** Adding the vectors directly causes scale mismatch, so each is L2-normalized first and then combined as $\mathbf e_q^{\rm final}={\rm L2Norm}(\tilde{\mathbf e}_q+\gamma\tilde{\mathbf e}_{\mathcal H})$, with a learnable scalar $\gamma$. Profile embeddings are computed in offline batch jobs, and a new click needs only $O(Kd)$ vector operations over a fixed window, with no LLM re-run, cheap enough for CPU.

**Dimension-flexible embeddings.** A Matryoshka loss trains jointly over prefix dimensions $\{200,256,512,1024\}$; at serving time embeddings are truncated to the target size without a separate model. The 200-dim prefix approximates the storage footprint of the 171-dim production embedding.

## 4. Experimental setup

Training uses DeepSpeed, bf16 and 8 GPUs, with temperature $\tau=0.02$. The authors note that fp16 mixed precision caused gradient overflow under DeepSpeed, so every reported model uses bf16. Data is split by time: the training set has 209K query-level instances involving 4.4M unique member profiles; the test set has 11.8K instances involving 93K profiles. There are two metrics: ACC checks whether the positive ranks first among 4 candidates (1 positive, 3 negatives; random is 0.25), and MAR@k checks whether clicked candidates land in the top k of a fixed 100-candidate pool. ACC saturates quickly, so MAR@k is the main signal.

## 5. Results

**Main offline results (Premium user retrieval):**

| Model | ACC | MAR@25 | MAR@100 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Holistic-171 (production) | 0.794 | 0.169 | 0.288 |
| Off-the-shelf 0.6B embedding | 0.771 | 0.100 | 0.192 |
| PAIR two-tower (no history) | 0.960 | 0.255 | 0.436 |
| + max-pooling history | 0.963 | 0.252 | 0.430 |
| + mean-pooling history | 0.965 | 0.253 | 0.430 |
| + GeM history | 0.966 | 0.264 | 0.447 |
| + attention history | 0.965 | 0.246 | 0.431 |
| + P-ATT history | 0.967 | 0.265 | 0.450 |

A few readings. **Preference fine-tuning is the main source of gain**: the two-tower model without history already reaches 0.436, 51% above the production baseline. **History adds a moderate extra gain**: P-ATT lifts 0.436 to 0.450, a 3.2% relative improvement, with GeM close behind (0.447). Notably, max pooling, mean pooling and position-free attention all fall slightly below the no-history model, so history signals must be fused carefully, not added indiscriminately. The authors therefore position the history tower mainly as a deployment-friendly mechanism for dynamic intent. Every PAIR variant exceeds 0.96 ACC, showing the 4-way task is nearly saturated.

**Dimensionality does not explain the gain.** Truncating the same Matryoshka model gives 0.421 at 200 dims, 0.432 at 256, 0.444 at 512 and 0.450 at 1024. At 256 dims, with 25% of the 1024-dim storage and about 0.40× relative latency, MAR@100 is still well above the 171-dim production embedding. The intended uses are 200 dims for candidate pre-filtering, 256 for latency-sensitive channels, 512 for standard retrieval and 1024 for Premium Browsemaps.

**Online A/B test.** The treatment uses 1024-dim PAIR embeddings with P-ATT history and the control uses production Holistic-171; both arms share the same downstream ranker to isolate the retrieval embedding. Traffic is split by user and stratified by subscription tier and activity level.

![Online A/B results (screenshot of the paper's Table 4): CTR +7.5% and Premium retention +2.1% (both significant under the production experimentation framework); page load latency +0.1% and recommendation coverage -0.2%.](figs/2610.30941/crop_tab4.png)

The authors discuss a gap: the offline relative MAR@100 gain is large, the online effect much smaller. That is expected in a multi-stage system: better retrieval improves the candidate set, while final engagement also depends on ranking, presentation and user context.

## 6. Limitations and what it means in practice

The paper lists its limitations: the A/B test used a fixed downstream ranker, and joint optimization of retrieval and ranking may add more; the experiment mainly measures short-term engagement and retention, while longer subscription effects need longer observation; the mixed-negative construction is a practical compromise, and a systematic comparison of random-only, exposure-only and ANN-mined negatives is still to do; and the test covered only Premium Browsemaps, so generalization to email recommendations, job matching and similar surfaces is unverified. Using exposure logs for negatives also carries the historical policy's bias into the model, as the authors themselves note.

For teams building recommendation retrieval, the paper offers several directly usable lessons. First, if your setting is **two-sided or complementary matching** (hiring, dating, B2B matchmaking, mentor matching), the "similar means relevant" assumption of general semantic embeddings may not hold, and fine-tuning with exposed-but-unclicked negatives is the cheapest, highest-yield step; in the paper it accounts for most of the gain. Second, to add real-time intent without running an LLM online, follow PAIR and make history a weighted sum of precomputed embeddings: query-agnostic positional attention, with $O(Kd)$ updates. ==First confirm that your history aggregation actually beats no history==; three common choices in the paper did worse. Third, when several surfaces share one model, Matryoshka training lets a single model cover multiple storage and latency budgets instead of maintaining several models.

papers.title: Ranking Bandits for Carousel Interfaces with Observable Browsing Depth
papers.authors: Takuma Yasuda, Atsuyoshi Nakamura, Dai Hai Nguyen
papers.abstract: Carousel interfaces allow a recommender system to directly observe how far a user has browsed. This signal distinguishes displayed but unclicked items from items that were never displayed, whereas conventional ranking-bandit models, including cascade and position-based models, generally treat examination as latent. We formulate a ranking-bandit problem in which a learner presents a list of $L$ items, observes the user's maximum browsing depth, and receives click feedback only for positions up to that depth. The objective is to maximize the expected number of clicks under an unknown item-attractiveness vector and a browsing-depth distribution. We propose three algorithms based on UCB, Thompson Sampling, and DMED, all of which update item statistics only from observed exposures. We derive an instance-dependent logarithmic upper bound for our UCB-based algorithm and an asymptotic upper bound for our DMED-based algorithm that coincides with the lower bound as its parameter $α\downarrow 0$, establishing asymptotic optimality in this limit. Simulations in synthetic shallow- and deep-browsing environments, together with experiments parameterized from RecGaze interaction logs, show that OD-TS attains final mean regret similar to PBM-TS, while the proposed methods achieve lower final mean regret than PBM-UCB.
papers.summary: In carousels and feeds users stop at a browsing depth; positions below that depth are neither clicked nor exposed, yet classical position-based models (PBM) still treat them as “seen but not clicked.” This paper proposes OD-UCB / OD-TS / OD-DMED under observable depth: update item stats only from truly exposed positions, with an instance-dependent log upper bound for OD-UCB. On synthetic shallow/deep environments and RecGaze-parameterized runs, OD-TS matches PBM-TS on final mean regret while all three beat PBM-UCB. ==When browse depth is observed, do not treat unseen slots as negative feedback==.

deep_reading.title: Ranking Bandits for Carousel Interfaces with Observable Browsing Depth
deep_reading.content:
Classic ranking bandits have an unavoidable blind spot: when a user does not click an item, the learner cannot tell "saw it and passed" from "never saw it". Cascade models and position-based models (PBM) treat examination as latent, and PBM must also separate position bias from item attractiveness, which costs statistical efficiency. In a horizontally scrolling carousel, however, client events can tell the system directly **how far the user browsed**. This paper formalizes that signal as a ranking-bandit problem and proposes three algorithms, OD-UCB, OD-TS and OD-DMED-L, that update only from confirmed exposures. Over 500,000 rounds in an environment calibrated from RecGaze eye-tracking logs, OD-TS reaches cumulative regret 856.1, comparable to PBM-TS given the true position biases (876.9), while PBM-UCB reaches 10,958.5. ==OD-TS needs neither the position biases nor the rejection sampling from a non-conjugate posterior that PBM-TS uses==. In theory, OD-DMED-L's asymptotic regret upper bound meets the lower bound as its parameter $\alpha\to0$, making it asymptotically optimal.

![Cumulative regret in the two synthetic environments (left: shallow browsing, right: deep browsing). Curves are means over 10 seeds; shading shows pointwise 95% confidence intervals.](figs/2610.05220/hf1.png)

## 1. The problem: turning "was it seen?" from a latent variable into an observation

Ranking bandits are the standard framework for balancing exploration and exploitation in recommendation and search: each round shows a ranked set of items and updates attractiveness estimates from clicks. Most methods build on click models:

| Property | Cascade | PBM | Observable depth (this paper) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Browsing depth | Latent | Latent | Observed as $V(t)$ |
| Click feedback | Up to first click | Per position | At displayed positions |
| Unseen positions | Partially observed | Censored | Explicitly excluded |
| Estimated quantities | Attractiveness | Attractiveness and position bias | Attractiveness |
| Update rule | Partial feedback | Bias correction | Exposure based |

An example shows the difference (illustrative). Suppose an item has been shown 1,000 times at position 5 and never clicked. Under PBM, the learner only knows that about $1000\times P_5$ of those showings were seen on average, and its attractiveness estimate must be corrected by the position bias. If $P_5$ is only 0.08, the effective sample is about 80, and the algorithm must first know or estimate $P_5$. If the logs record how far each session actually scrolled, you can count only those roughly 80 confirmed exposures and get a clean Bernoulli sample mean directly.

Client events in carousels and scrollable lists can record the farthest position actually displayed, which the authors call **browsing depth**. At or above that depth, both clicks and confirmed non-clicks are observed; deeper positions are left out. Unexposed items are therefore never mixed in as negatives.

## 2. Problem setting

There are $K$ items, and each round $t$ shows a ranking $\boldsymbol a(t)$ of $L<K$ distinct items. The user always sees the first, keeps going down, and stops after the $V(t)$-th. $V(t)$ is i.i.d. and **independent of the display order**. Let $P_j=\Pr\{V(t)\ge j\}$ be the probability that position $j$ is seen, with $1=P_1\ge\cdots\ge P_L>0$. Each seen item $i$ is clicked independently with unknown probability $\theta_i$, a simple multi-click model chosen to isolate the value of depth observation itself.

The reward is the number of clicks, with expectation $\mu(\boldsymbol a)=\sum_{j=1}^L P_j\theta_{a_j}$. Assuming $\theta_1>\theta_2>\cdots>\theta_K$ (unknown to the learner), the optimal ranking puts the top $L$ items in descending order of attractiveness. Regret is ${\rm Reg}_A(T)=\sum_t\Delta_{\boldsymbol a(t)}$, the sum of per-round gaps to the optimal expected reward.

## 3. Three algorithms, all updating only from confirmed exposure

All three share one update subroutine: given the user's depth $V$ and clicks on the first $V$ positions, update the exposure count $n_i$ and click count $s_i$ of only those $V$ items. Because updates happen only after confirmed exposure, $\hat\theta_i=s_i/n_i$ is a direct sample mean of a Bernoulli parameter, with no position-bias correction.

- **OD-UCB**: score $\hat\theta_i+\sqrt{\alpha\log t/n_i}$, infinite for never-exposed items; show the $L$ highest.
- **OD-TS**: a ${\rm Beta}(1,1)$ prior per item gives posterior ${\rm Beta}(1+s_i,1+n_i-s_i)$; each round, sample from the posteriors and show the $L$ highest samples. Because exposure is confirmed, the posterior stays conjugate and sampling is very cheap.
- **OD-DMED-L**: adapted from DMED. It first rotates through items so each is exposed at least once. Afterwards, when the exploration queue is empty, it shows the $L$ items with the highest sample means and checks every item $i$ outside the current top $L$ against $n_i\,d(\hat\theta_i,\hat\theta_{a_L})<(1+\alpha)\log(t-1)$, where $d$ is the Bernoulli KL divergence; items that pass get a ranking enqueued for exploration (first $L-1$ unchanged, last slot replaced by $i$). Intuitively, it asks "are we confident enough that $i$ is worse than the $L$-th item?" and, if not, gives it another try in the last slot.

The three differ mainly in how they explore. OD-UCB explores optimistically with upper confidence bounds and is the simplest to implement; OD-TS explores through posterior randomness and performs best at finite horizons in the experiments; OD-DMED-L explores only items with insufficient information, allocating exploration by KL divergence, which is why it can be asymptotically optimal. In all three, exploration competes with the optimal set only at position $L$: to decide whether an item belongs in the top $L$, what matters is its gap to the $L$-th item, $\Delta_i=\theta_L-\theta_i$.

## 4. Theoretical results

**Lower bound (Theorem 1).** For any strongly consistent learner, $\liminf_{T\to\infty}\mathbb E[{\rm Reg}(T)]/\log T\ge\sum_{i=L+1}^K\Delta_i/d(\theta_i,\theta_L)$, where $\Delta_i=\theta_L-\theta_i$.

**Finite-time upper bound for OD-UCB (Theorem 2).** For $\alpha>1/2$, regret grows as $\log T$, with a leading term containing $\sum_{i>L}1/(P_L\Delta_i)$. The authors compare it with Lagrée et al.'s bound for PBM-UCB with known position biases: in comparable limits, PBM-UCB's leading term carries an extra factor of $P_L^{-2}$. When the last displayed position is rarely seen (small $P_L$), PBM-style bounds degrade sharply, which depth observation avoids. The authors also note that, by Pinsker's inequality, the $\log T$ coefficient of the OD-UCB bound is not asymptotically optimal.

**Asymptotic upper bound for OD-DMED-L (Theorem 3).** For any $\alpha>0$, $\limsup\mathbb E[{\rm Reg}(T)]/\log T\le(1+\alpha)\sum_{j>L}\Delta_j/d(\theta_j,\theta_L)$. As $\alpha\to0$ this meets the lower bound, so the algorithm is asymptotically optimal in that limit.

## 5. Experiments

The setup is $K=50$, $L=5$, $T=500{,}000$, with three environments. The **shallow** synthetic environment has exposure probabilities 1.00, 0.55, 0.30, 0.15, 0.08; the **deep** one has 1.00, 0.80, 0.70, 0.60, 0.50. The **RecGaze-calibrated** environment comes from a dataset recording eye tracking, clicks, cursor movement and explanations for carousel interactions (87 participants, 3 movie-selection tasks, 3,477 interactions). Processing yields 23,075 usable observations; the 50 most-exposed items (85–87 confirmed exposures each) and the first 5 positions are kept, giving exposure probabilities 1.0000, 0.9031, 0.8529, 0.7720, 0.6879, with Laplace-smoothed click rates. Baselines are PBM-UCB and PBM-TS (given the true position biases $P_j$ but not the realized depth) and LastClick-UCB (positions up to the last click count as exposed; with no click, the whole list counts as exposed). Within each seed, all methods share the same depth and click random draws.

**Mean cumulative regret at 500,000 rounds:**

| Method | Shallow | Deep | RecGaze-calibrated |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| OD-TS | 1,121.8 | 1,326.9 | 856.1 |
| PBM-TS (known $P_j$) | 1,159.9 | 1,356.8 | 876.9 |
| OD-DMED-L | 2,137.2 | 4,006.6 | 1,910.5 |
| OD-UCB | 6,280.6 | 8,761.5 | 8,532.1 |
| LastClick-UCB | 8,594.8 | 9,819.1 | 19,580.5 |
| PBM-UCB (known $P_j$) | 19,568.2 | 12,226.3 | 10,958.5 |

OD-TS and PBM-TS have overlapping confidence intervals in all three environments, but PBM-TS needs the true marginal exposure probabilities. All three observable-depth methods beat PBM-UCB and LastClick-UCB in every environment. The shallow-versus-deep comparison suggests that the faster exposure decays with position, the more depth observation helps: PBM-UCB's regret is about 3.1× OD-UCB's in the shallow environment and about 1.4× in the deep one.

![Cumulative regret in the RecGaze-calibrated environment, mean over 30 seeds, with pointwise 95% confidence intervals shaded.](figs/2610.05220/hf2.png)

**Asymptotic behavior.** To test the theory, the deep environment is run to $T=10^7$. For this instance the Theorem 1 coefficient is 218.45, and the OD-DMED-L reference is $(1+\alpha)\times218.45=240.30$ ($\alpha=0.1$). OD-DMED-L's ${\rm Reg}(t)/\log t$ peaks at 291.78 near $t\approx5.09\times10^5$ and falls to 261.30 at $10^7$, moving toward 240.30. The median information allocation is 1.102 near $10^6$ (close to the threshold 1.1) and 1.053 at $10^7$, between the threshold and the lower-bound target of 1.

![Asymptotic behavior in the deep environment. Left: mean Reg(t)/log t with 95% confidence intervals. Right: median information allocation of OD-DMED-L over seeds and suboptimal items, with the 10–90% range shaded.](figs/2610.05220/hf3.png)

## 6. Limitations and what it means in practice

The authors state the limitations clearly. Clicks are assumed independent, and browsing depth is assumed independent of display order. The RecGaze experiment is a model-driven simulation calibrated from logs, not an online deployment, and does not establish regret under real user behavior. The high click rates of a few items may reflect task-specific intent rather than context-free attractiveness. RecGaze's exposure is even deeper than the deep synthetic environment, so its differences cannot be attributed to browsing depth alone. Future work includes relaxing the assumptions, online validation, a sharper OD-UCB analysis, and finite-time guarantees for OD-DMED-L and OD-TS.

In practice, the assumption that depth is independent of order may not hold: very attractive content near the front might make users scroll farther, or click and leave. The paper does not handle this dependence.

For recommendation teams, the most direct lesson is to **check whether your logs already contain exposure depth**. Many carousel, horizontal-scroll and feed clients already report visible positions or scroll depth, yet offline training and online exploration still treat shown-but-unseen items as negatives. In bandit or cold-start exploration, updating only from confirmed exposure and running Thompson sampling with a conjugate Beta posterior is simple to implement and needs no position-bias estimate; in the paper it matches PBM-TS given the true position biases. A rollout can go in three steps. First, store the farthest visible position of each impression as a log field aligned with click events. Second, compute empirical exposure probabilities per position offline and see how fast they decay; the faster the decay, the more confirmed exposure pays off. Third, swap the update rule on exploration traffic first and compare cumulative clicks against the existing PBM or last-click rule. Also note that the paper assumes depth is independent of order, so before launch check that the depth distribution is stable across rankings. ==The signal is worth most on interfaces where exposure decays quickly with position, such as mobile horizontal scrolling==.
deep_reading.content_html:
Classic ranking bandits have an unavoidable blind spot: when a user does not click an item, the learner cannot tell "saw it and passed" from "never saw it". Cascade models and position-based models (PBM) treat examination as latent, and PBM must also separate position bias from item attractiveness, which costs statistical efficiency. In a horizontally scrolling carousel, however, client events can tell the system directly how far the user browsed. This paper formalizes that signal as a ranking-bandit problem and proposes three algorithms, OD-UCB, OD-TS and OD-DMED-L, that update only from confirmed exposures. Over 500,000 rounds in an environment calibrated from RecGaze eye-tracking logs, OD-TS reaches cumulative regret 856.1, comparable to PBM-TS given the true position biases (876.9), while PBM-UCB reaches 10,958.5. OD-TS needs neither the position biases nor the rejection sampling from a non-conjugate posterior that PBM-TS uses. In theory, OD-DMED-L's asymptotic regret upper bound meets the lower bound as its parameter α→0, making it asymptotically optimal.

1. The problem: turning "was it seen?" from a latent variable into an observation

Ranking bandits are the standard framework for balancing exploration and exploitation in recommendation and search: each round shows a ranked set of items and updates attractiveness estimates from clicks. Most methods build on click models:

PropertyCascadePBMObservable depth (this paper)
Browsing depthLatentLatentObserved as $V(t)$
Click feedbackUp to first clickPer positionAt displayed positions
Unseen positionsPartially observedCensoredExplicitly excluded
Estimated quantitiesAttractivenessAttractiveness and position biasAttractiveness
Update rulePartial feedbackBias correctionExposure based

An example shows the difference (illustrative). Suppose an item has been shown 1,000 times at position 5 and never clicked. Under PBM, the learner only knows that about 1000×P5​ of those showings were seen on average, and its attractiveness estimate must be corrected by the position bias. If P5​ is only 0.08, the effective sample is about 80, and the algorithm must first know or estimate P5​. If the logs record how far each session actually scrolled, you can count only those roughly 80 confirmed exposures and get a clean Bernoulli sample mean directly.

Client events in carousels and scrollable lists can record the farthest position actually displayed, which the authors call browsing depth. At or above that depth, both clicks and confirmed non-clicks are observed; deeper positions are left out. Unexposed items are therefore never mixed in as negatives.

2. Problem setting

There are K items, and each round t shows a ranking a(t) of $L<K$ distinct items. The user always sees the first, keeps going down, and stops after the $V(t)$-th. $V(t)$ is i.i.d. and independent of the display order. Let Pj​=Pr{V(t)≥j} be the probability that position j is seen, with 1=P1​≥⋯≥PL​>0. Each seen item i is clicked independently with unknown probability θi​, a simple multi-click model chosen to isolate the value of depth observation itself.

The reward is the number of clicks, with expectation μ(a)=∑j=1L​Pj​θaj​​. Assuming θ1​>θ2​>⋯>θK​ (unknown to the learner), the optimal ranking puts the top L items in descending order of attractiveness. Regret is RegA​(T)=∑t​Δa(t)​, the sum of per-round gaps to the optimal expected reward.

3. Three algorithms, all updating only from confirmed exposure

All three share one update subroutine: given the user's depth V and clicks on the first V positions, update the exposure count ni​ and click count si​ of only those V items. Because updates happen only after confirmed exposure, θ^i​=si​/ni​ is a direct sample mean of a Bernoulli parameter, with no position-bias correction.

  • OD-UCB: score θ^i​+αlogt/ni​​, infinite for never-exposed items; show the L highest.
  • OD-TS: a Beta(1,1) prior per item gives posterior Beta(1+si​,1+ni​−si​); each round, sample from the posteriors and show the L highest samples. Because exposure is confirmed, the posterior stays conjugate and sampling is very cheap.
  • OD-DMED-L: adapted from DMED. It first rotates through items so each is exposed at least once. Afterwards, when the exploration queue is empty, it shows the L items with the highest sample means and checks every item i outside the current top L against ni​d(θ^i​,θ^aL​​)<(1+α)log(t−1), where d is the Bernoulli KL divergence; items that pass get a ranking enqueued for exploration (first $L-1$ unchanged, last slot replaced by i). Intuitively, it asks "are we confident enough that i is worse than the L-th item?" and, if not, gives it another try in the last slot.

The three differ mainly in how they explore. OD-UCB explores optimistically with upper confidence bounds and is the simplest to implement; OD-TS explores through posterior randomness and performs best at finite horizons in the experiments; OD-DMED-L explores only items with insufficient information, allocating exploration by KL divergence, which is why it can be asymptotically optimal. In all three, exploration competes with the optimal set only at position L: to decide whether an item belongs in the top L, what matters is its gap to the L-th item, Δi​=θL​−θi​.

4. Theoretical results

Lower bound (Theorem 1). For any strongly consistent learner, liminfT→∞​E[Reg(T)]/logT≥∑i=L+1K​Δi​/d(θi​,θL​), where Δi​=θL​−θi​.

Finite-time upper bound for OD-UCB (Theorem 2). For α>1/2, regret grows as logT, with a leading term containing ∑i>L​1/(PL​Δi​). The authors compare it with Lagrée et al.'s bound for PBM-UCB with known position biases: in comparable limits, PBM-UCB's leading term carries an extra factor of PL−2​. When the last displayed position is rarely seen (small PL​), PBM-style bounds degrade sharply, which depth observation avoids. The authors also note that, by Pinsker's inequality, the logT coefficient of the OD-UCB bound is not asymptotically optimal.

Asymptotic upper bound for OD-DMED-L (Theorem 3). For any α>0, limsupE[Reg(T)]/logT≤(1+α)∑j>L​Δj​/d(θj​,θL​). As α→0 this meets the lower bound, so the algorithm is asymptotically optimal in that limit.

papers.title: Bezier-Guided Adaptive Flow for Cross-domain Sequential Recommendation
papers.authors: Ziang Lu, Yu Zhang, Xinzhe Jiang, Lei Sang, Yiwen Zhang
papers.abstract: Cross-domain sequential recommendation aims to alleviate data sparsity and cold-start problems by transferring useful preference knowledge across domains. However, users exhibit varying degrees of preference consistency across domains, while existing methods often rely on global alignment objectives or coarse-grained transfer strategies. Such approaches may introduce irrelevant information and provide limited flexibility in adapting semantic representations to individual user preferences. To address these challenges, we propose BGAFlow, a personalized framework that combines state-adaptive semantic evolution with user-specific transfer control. BGAFlow first establishes a shared semantic space through unified dual-domain pretraining with user profiles inferred by a large language model (LLM). Based on latent interest overlap, it then estimates a personalized horizon to determine the appropriate transfer extent for each user. To enable semantic adaptation, BGAFlow constructs a conditional Bezier curve as a geometric reference and learns a residual flow that progressively refines the trajectory based on intermediate preference states. The learned flow incorporates dynamic preference feedback to adjust transfer directions, while recommendation supervision and trajectory regularization encourage effective and smooth adaptation. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that BGAFlow consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, validating the benefits of personalized transfer control and state-adaptive semantic evolution.
papers.summary: Cross-domain sequential recommenders often move preference via global alignment and ignore how consistent a user is across domains, so irrelevant semantics leak in. BGAFlow builds a shared semantic space, evolves it with state-adaptive semantics, and gates transfer per user so the amount of transfer scales with that user’s cross-domain consistency instead of one global objective. ==Transfer granularity belongs at “how consistent is this user across these two domains,” not at one global alignment loss==.

papers.title: Behavior lifetime modeling uses time sensitive behavioral signals to rank candidate items for purchase in E commerce recommendation
company: Jiangxi University of Software Professional Technology
papers.abstract:
Multi-behavior recommendation relies on heterogeneous user actions to infer purchase intent, but the purchase relevance of browsing, favoriting, and add-to-cart behaviors can change over time and become stale before prediction. To address this problem, we propose behavior lifetime modeling-based recommendation (BLMRec), a candidate-item purchase ranking framework that explicitly models the temporal validity of historical behaviors.
BLMRec encodes each behavior according to its type and temporal distance from the prediction moment, and employs multi-window lifetime learning to estimate both short-term activation and long-term persistence. The resulting temporal validity and stagnation signals are used to suppress outdated auxiliary behaviors.
BLMRec further performs candidate-conditioned matching between historical and candidate items through category, co-occurrence, co-purchase, and behavior-transition relations, followed by purchase-intent calibration for final ranking. Experiments on Taobao UserBehavior and RetailRocket, with 33.5 M and 1.35 M interactions after preprocessing, show that BLMRec improves Recall@20/NDCG@20 over the strongest baseline by 6.0%/7.3% and 6.9%/9.2%, respectively.
Further analyses indicate that the gains are associated with improved suppression of stale, weakly related, and high-auxiliary non-conversion signals.
papers.summary: In multi-behavior recommendation, how much browse / favorite / add-to-cart still predict purchase can go stale before the prediction moment. BLMRec encodes each behavior by type and temporal distance from prediction time, uses multi-window lifetime learning for short-term activation and long-term persistence, then feeds validity and stagnation signals into candidate purchase ranking so expired actions are not treated as strong intent. ==Behaviors are not permanent labels—model a lifetime per behavior type or ranking gets pulled by stale signals==.

papers.title: MAPS: A Multi-Agent Personalized Script-Driven Video Advertising System Enhanced by Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Zhongyu Wang, Chen Zuo, Qingxuan Sun, Jiayang Qiao, Qiuhao Qian, Songyan Cui, Guocheng Chen
papers.abstract: With the rapid growth of online video consumption, video advertising has become a dominant component of digital advertising. Most personalized video advertising systems follow a retrieval-based paradigm, which matches ad content with user preferences in a feature space and recommends the most similar candidates. However, since the candidate creatives are pre-produced, this paradigm limits the granularity of personalization and leads to performance disparities across diverse user groups. To address this limitation, we propose a multi-agent personalized script-driven video advertising system (MAPS). We design four collaborative agents that form a closed-loop pipeline of user profile modeling, script generation, video synthesis, and feedback-driven iterative refinement. To train the Scripter Agent, we develop a reinforcement learning framework equipped with a multi-dimensional reward function, which steers the agent toward producing scripts that simultaneously align with user content preferences and target product information. Extensive offline experiments on representative datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves encouraging performance in generating and integrating personalized creatives. Online A/B experiments in a specific scenario in the Kuaishou advertising system show that MAPS improves CTR by 2.87%, CVR by 2.74%, and ARPU by 9.85% over the generative baseline.
papers.summary: Most personalized video ads still retrieve among pre-produced creatives, so personalization stays coarse and gaps across user groups persist. Kuaishou’s MAPS runs four collaborative agents (profile → script → creative → closed loop) to generate script-driven video ads per user; versus a retrieval baseline, CTR +2.87%, CVR +2.74%, ARPU +9.85%. ==When personalization is capped by pre-produced creatives, put creative production inside a multi-agent loop instead of chasing similarity in feature space==.

papers.title: UserArena: Benchmarking Interactive User Simulation for Long-Horizon Shopping Agents
papers.authors: Jujia Zhao, Jiakai Tang, Jing Yu, Wen Chen, Jian Wu, Han Zhu, Fei Sun, Suzan Verberne, Zhaochun Ren
papers.abstract: Agentic recommendation pursues shopper goals through sequences of context-dependent decisions. Developing and evaluating such policies requires faithful recommendation world models that capture both the interactive shopping environment and users' behavioral responses over long interactions. Existing resources rarely provide long-horizon, fine-grained real-user trajectories or support trajectory-level evaluation and offline validation against production A/B results. We introduce UserArena, a real-world e-commerce interactive benchmark containing 64,729 session trajectories from 11,010 users, spanning 566,102 items and 13 action types. UserArena pairs these trajectories with an interactive environment and supports offline validation against outcomes from a controlled production A/B test, enabling five-level evaluation from output validity and local decisions to sequential behavior, personalization, and outcomes. To improve simulator fidelity over these long-horizon interactions, we further propose On-Policy Trajectory Distillation (OPTD), which uses trajectory-level intent to provide dense teacher targets on student-generated rollouts. Experiments show that OPTD achieves the strongest overall fidelity among the evaluated simulators under UserArena's evaluation protocol and most closely reproduces the production policy effect in offline simulation.
papers.summary: Agentic shopping recommenders need world models that hold over long interactions, yet few resources offer fine-grained real-user trajectories or offline checks against production A/B. UserArena releases 64,729 session trajectories from 11,010 users (566,102 items, 13 action types), paired with an interactive environment and trajectory-level evaluation for offline policies vs production A/B. ==Without long-horizon real trajectories and an A/B anchor, agent recommendation “world models” only look good in toy sims==.

papers.title: FairFRESH: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Fair and Explainable Household Food Recommendation
papers.authors: Kodur Sai Vinay Sathvik, Kakoli Bora, Tejaswini R. M
papers.abstract: Recommender systems typically serve one user at a time. However, in households, members share a finite pantry and follow different dietary rules, making independent recommendations prone to resource conflicts and dietary violations. We formulate household food recommendation as constrained fair division and present FairFRESH, a neuro-symbolic framework that learns per-member utilities, allocates foods under explicit welfare objectives, enforces dietary rules through a deterministic filter, and explains recommendations using Shapley and Banzhaf attributions. Theoretically, we show that no finite penalty guarantees compliance near a dietary-rule threshold, establish approximation guarantees for greedy allocation under utilitarian and smoothed Nash objectives in the stock-free model before filtering, and characterize the scale invariance of Nash welfare. We also use the minimax theorem to analyze rotating shared meals. On NHANES-derived data, the learned utility model achieves Recall@20 of 0.293, outperforming five learned recommenders (at most 0.244) but not a previous-day repetition heuristic (0.321). On held-out four-person households, Nash allocation reduces Gini disparity by 42% relative to conflict resolution while improving Recall@20 from 0.180 to 0.197. It comes within 2% of an upper bound on the smoothed Nash optimum, and rescaling one member's utilities changes at most 1.5% of assignments. All recommendations satisfy the encoded dietary rules, while attribution scores correlate with utility loss upon component removal (r = 0.76). In simulation, shared meals reduce pantry use by about one-third, and weekly rotation increases the worst-off member's utility by 38% over the best fixed meal.
papers.summary: Households share a pantry and members follow different dietary rules, so per-person recommenders collide on resources and break constraints. FairFRESH casts household food recommendation as constrained fair division: learn per-member utilities, allocate under welfare objectives, enforce diet rules with a deterministic filter, and explain with Shapley/Banzhaf. Learned utilities hit Recall@20 0.293; fair allocation cuts Gini disparity 42% vs conflict resolution, lifts Recall@20 from 0.180 to 0.197 (within ~2% of a smoothed Nash upper bound), and every recommendation satisfies the rules. ==The hard constraints are shared stock and diet rules—after utility learning you still need an enforceable filter==.

papers.title: Truthful by Omission: Click Thinning for LLM-Native Advertising
papers.authors: Junhua Liu, Zhicheng Liang, Zejun Zhang, Langzhou He, Feng Qian
papers.abstract: Generative AI assistants are becoming an advertising medium, embedding sponsored content in their answers. This setting departs from classical position auctions in two ways: an ad's click-through rate depends on the passage that hosts it, and because users stop at their first click, earlier ads take clicks from later ones. This competition for clicks makes truthfulness delicate: a higher bid can reshape the allocation and put a competitor ahead of the bidder, reducing the bidder's clicks. Existing mechanisms either attain a constant fraction of the optimal welfare (advertisers' total click value) but are not known to be truthful, or are truthful but their welfare guarantee degrades as the number of passages grows. We achieve both even when the answer and its editorial order are fixed before bidding. Assuming each ad's click-through rate when reached is known and unaffected by omitting other ads, we give a computationally efficient mechanism that is truthful in expectation and attains at least half the optimal welfare under free reordering. Our key idea, click thinning, omits ads at random, showing earlier ads less often so that each ad's overall click probability no longer depends on the order of the ads. Welfare maximization then reduces to a tractable matching problem, and solving it exactly with VCG-style payments makes truthful bidding optimal in expectation. Characterizing the click probabilities that omission can achieve sharpens the approximation factor from $2$ to $2-(1-δ)^{K-1}$ when at most $K$ ads are shown and each click-through rate is at most $δ$. This factor is the best possible for any order-preserving rule, even one that ignores incentives and computation, so truthfulness and computational efficiency incur no additional worst-case loss.
papers.summary: Generative assistants now host ads inside answers: an ad’s CTR depends on the hosting passage, and because users often stop at the first click, earlier ads steal clicks from later ones—raising a bid can even push a rival ahead of you. Existing mechanisms either approximate welfare but lack known truthfulness, or are truthful while welfare degrades with more ads. This paper redesigns the mechanism for that click competition, folding passage dependence and early-stop externalities into allocation and payment. ==In-assistant ads are not a drop-in position auction—passage sets CTR and early stop creates externalities, so truthfulness and welfare must be rebuilt together==.

papers.title: From Scores to Safe Sets: Exact Safety--Constrained Decoding for Medication Recommendation
papers.authors: Animesh Agarwal, Meysam Ghaffari, Nina Fatehi, Anushka Swarup, Carlos Morato
papers.abstract: Recent generative medication recommendation systems ultimately produce sets of drugs, but drug--drug interaction (DDI) constraints depend on the set as a whole. A natural post-hoc approach is to first predict medications and then locally repair interacting pairs by removing one drug at a time. We ask whether this local repair step itself introduces avoidable error. Using fixed medication scores from FLAME's frozen classifier on MIMIC-III, we compare increasingly strong local repair strategies with an exact global decoder while holding the scores, output size, and DDI constraint fixed. The global decoder jointly selects the highest-scoring feasible medication set using mixed-integer linear programming. Across validation and test splits, global decoding consistently achieves higher Jaccard similarity than greedy repair, degree-aware repair, and degree-aware repair strengthened with exhaustive 1-swap local search. Its advantage is small under loose DDI constraints and becomes larger as the constraint tightens; on the test split it reaches +0.0064 Jaccard over the strongest local baseline at the strict DDI operating point. The finding also holds across a fine accuracy--DDI sweep at matched realized DDI exposure and under three score representations. At the strict setting, global decoding retains more true-positive medications while removing more false positives. These results show that medication recommendation is not only a representation-learning problem: even with a frozen clinical model, how its scores are converted into a constrained medication set can materially affect the final prediction.
papers.summary: Generative medication recommenders ultimately emit drug sets, and DDI constraints act on the whole set; the usual fix is predict-then locally delete interacting drugs. Holding FLAME’s frozen MIMIC-III scores, output size, and DDI constraint fixed, this paper compares stronger local repair strategies against an exact global MILP decoder that jointly picks the highest-scoring feasible set: local repair itself adds avoidable error; global decoding is stabler. ==Do not rely on post-hoc local repair for set-level constraints—with scores fixed, a global feasible decoder removes the extra error local repair introduces==.

papers.title: FAIRGate: Agentic Runtime Policy Selection and Verified Repair for Fairer Recommendation Delivery
papers.authors: Navkar Jain, Enock Ayiku, Kenneth Fletcher
papers.abstract: Fairness-aware recommender systems often encode one fairness objective during training or apply a fixed re-ranking rule after scoring. In deployment, however, the appropriate fairness action can vary across requests because the candidate pool, item metadata, exposure debt, user preference history, and utility budget all change at runtime. We propose FAIRGate, a model-agnostic delivery controller that places an agentic policy-selection layer between a base ranker and the final top-K list. The agent does not define fairness objectives from scratch. It chooses from a predefined policy library covering long-tail exposure, item-group exposure balance, concentration control, calibration protection, and abstention. A deterministic executor then applies the selected policy through constrained repair, and a validator accepts the result only when relevance, feasibility, metadata, calibration, and audit constraints are satisfied. The final language-model component receives only the verified audit trace and produces evidence-linked narration after the ranking decision is fixed. This design gives the agent runtime responsibility while keeping fairness enforcement measurable, bounded, and replayable.
papers.summary: Fairness-aware recommenders often bake one objective into training or apply a fixed re-rank after scoring; in production the right action changes with the candidate pool, exposure debt, preference history, and utility budget. FAIRGate inserts a model-agnostic policy-selection agent between the base ranker and the final top-K, choosing from a predefined library (long-tail exposure, group balance, concentration control, calibration protection, …) per request instead of inventing fairness on the fly. ==Deployed fairness is “which validated policy to pick,” not redefining fairness on every request==.
